title: For Whom Does AI Feedback Support Writing Self-Efficacy? The Role of Students’ Achievement Goal Orientation and Writing Skills

source.title: For Whom Does AI Feedback Support Writing Self-Efficacy? The Role of Students’ Achievement Goal Orientation and Writing Skills
source.authors: Thorben Jansen, Hannah Pünjer, Mira Tanz, Nils-Jonathan Schaller, Lars Höft

studies.title: Classroom study · AI feedback versus self-feedback

fields.label: Question
fields.value: For which secondary school students does AI feedback support confidence in argumentative writing more than guided self-feedback?

fields.label: What the paper covers
fields.value: A classroom study and a separate Bench adaptation. The published outcome is writing self-efficacy, distinct from scored essay quality.

fields.label: Across the paper
fields.value: There was little average difference in writing self-efficacy. The pattern varied with students’ goals and, for mastery orientation, baseline writing skill.

fields.label: Expectation or comparison
fields.value: The authors predicted that the effect of AI feedback versus self-feedback would vary with students’ goals and explored whether baseline writing skill further changed it.

fields.label: Interpretation and limits
fields.value: The article reports 805 students from 47 classes. The community adaptation uses 801 cases, changed class handling and goal-item counts, a substitute scorer and reconstructed feedback settings. Its run is not historical replication.
fields.derivation: Scope of the published evidence and, where linked, differences from the Bench adaptation.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Students wrote an argumentative text in five parts and received either AI-generated feedback or self-feedback prompts. The analysis measures writing self-efficacy and examines baseline writing skill and four goal orientations: mastery, performance approach, performance avoidance and work avoidance.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: The paper reports one feedback event per writing part. The comparison concerns immediate self-efficacy in this specific classroom workflow.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Model interactions between feedback condition and goal orientation, including baseline writing skill. Compare average and conditional effects.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: The paper reports a near-zero average contrast. Students higher in performance approach or avoidance showed lower self-efficacy with AI feedback relative to self-feedback, with stronger evidence for avoidance. Work avoidance did not show a clear interaction. The mastery pattern depended on writing skill, but was sensitive to how standard errors were estimated.
